motivo: Reportaje de reserva, sin mensajes de la semana, con tema y enfoque del jefe de reportajes (2099-02-01-tema.json): enseñar al alumnado a tratar la respuesta de un chatbot como una pista que se comprueba, no como una fuente. Parte de la guía de la UNESCO «AI answers. You decide» (Biblioteca, 12-11-2026), que solo tuvo un artículo de Biblioteca, y la sitúa en los marcos que ya piden esa competencia (OCDE y Comisión Europea, PISA 2029, DigComp 3.0, currículo LOMLOE, guías española y catalana), con datos de estudios y práctica de aula gratuita. No caduca en un mes y no repite los reportajes anteriores (agentes, edad, detectores): esos tratan qué permitir y cómo evaluar; este, qué enseñar.
titular: A chatbot’s answer is a lead, not a source, and checking it is taught in class
entradilla: Chatbots answer with a confidence that does not always match what they say, and their own makers warn of it. This report explains why that happens, what UNESCO and the European and Spanish frameworks propose for teaching students to check, what studies say about students, and how to work on it in a single session in any subject, at no cost and without students needing an account.

parrafos: A language model does not consult a database of facts: it produces the text that, according to the patterns it has learned, is the most plausible continuation of a question. That is why it can write a correct fact, an outdated one and an invented one with equal ease. The UNESCO guide that runs through this report sums it up in one idea: fluency is not the same as accuracy. It adds a nuance that affects every classroom: a search engine shows a list of pages, by different authors who sometimes disagree, whereas a chatbot delivers a single synthesised answer that can hide where each claim comes from and what disagreements there were along the way.

This is not a flaw that will disappear with the next version. In the preprint “[LLMs Will Always Hallucinate, and We Need to Live With This](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05746)”, published on arXiv in September 2024, Sourav Banerjee, Ayushi Agarwal and Saloni Singla argue that hallucinations (false statements presented as true) are an inevitable feature of these systems. In ChatGPT-IA-edu, the teachers’ group where the work was shared, one message summed up what it implies according to the authors: [human verification is needed, and results must be checked against reliable sources](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/14006). In another conversation the idea was taken to voice assistants, based on a study of their credibility: [a convincing voice does not make what it says more reliable](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/30445), and sources should be checked when the AI speaks without visible references.

The companies themselves acknowledge it in their help centres. On the page “[Claude is providing incorrect or misleading responses. What's going on?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8525154-claude-is-providing-incorrect-or-misleading-responses-what-s-going-on)”, Anthropic explains that making up information, known as hallucinating, is a consequence of the models’ current limitations, and warns: “Users should not rely on Claude as a singular source of truth”. When the answer comes from a web search, it asks users to review the cited sources, because the original pages may contain context that the summary leaves out.

Google says something similar about Gemini in “[Learn about responses from Gemini Apps](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16279220?hl=en)”: “Gemini can hallucinate and present inaccurate information as factual”, and it recommends double-checking in particular what it says about people. Its page on [related sources](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/14143489?hl=en) makes clear that not every answer comes with links: if the sources button does not appear, that answer offers none. **That an answer cites sources helps in checking it, but does not make it correct**: checking remains the job of the person reading.

On 10 November 2026 UNESCO presented “[AI answers. You decide: A companion guide to the UNESCO media and information literacy curriculum](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000400013)”, by Anne Leppäjärvi, a guide for teachers that complements its 2021 media and information literacy curriculum. It is in English; according to the [organisation’s announcement](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-answers-you-decide-unesco-launches-new-media-and-information-literacy-curriculum), it is organised into five areas, from AI in everyday life to the future, and according to the [UNESCO Institute for Information Technologies in Education](https://iite.unesco.org/announcements/unesco-s-guide-on-media-and-information-literacy-in-ai-infused-information-environments-for-educators/) it is designed mainly for students aged 13 to 15, with scope for adapting it to other ages. The document is also in the [ChatGPT-IA-edu digital Library](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/21753/54308), and the paper explained its contents in [a Library article on the guide](pieza:2026-11-12/unesco-ia-decides).

Its proposal fits on a card. For any piece of content, five questions: who made it, what evidence backs it, what system shaped it, who benefits from it being believed or shared, and what needs to be verified before acting. For an AI answer, a gradation according to what is at stake: trust, verify or question. Asking for a synonym is not the same as asking for a dose, an exam date or a fact that is going to be published. And a rule that the guide states literally: “treat an AI-generated answer as a lead rather than a source”.

The guide adds three self-check questions, among them whether you are learning or just obtaining a result, and argues that not using AI in an activity is a legitimate decision, as long as it does not mean giving up on understanding it. It has limits: it is long, it is written for an international audience, and several of its legal examples do not apply to the Spanish context.

apartados.ladillo: A competence already in the frameworks
parrafos: Checking what AI says is not one guide’s whim. The AI literacy framework for primary and secondary education from the OECD and the European Commission, “Empowering Learners for the Age of AI”, presented in Brussels on 18 June 2026 according to the European [Digital Skills and Jobs Platform](https://digital-skills-jobs.europa.eu/en/latest/news/new-ai-literacy-framework-common-reference-integrating-ai-literacy-education), brings together nineteen competences. One of them, in the [interactive version of the framework](https://ailiteracyframework.org/frameworks/), consists of evaluating whether an AI answer should be accepted, revised or rejected, at three levels: understanding why it must be verified and how; checking it against reliable sources and against what the task requires; and justifying the decision. According to the [framework’s website](https://ailiteracyframework.org/), it contributes to the innovative domain of the PISA 2029 assessment, devoted to media and AI literacy.

In the European Union, Article 4 of the [AI Act](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-4) has required organisations that use AI systems, since 2 February 2025, to promote AI literacy among their staff; on its [page on talent, skills and literacy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-talent-skills-and-literacy), updated on 13 October 2026, the Commission states that the Digital Omnibus amendment, in force since mid-July 2026, does not require any specific level of literacy from anyone. The obligation covers the staff of a school that uses these tools, not students. The European digital competence framework, [DigComp 3.0](https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-news-and-updates/european-commission-updates-its-digital-competence-framework-digcomp-2025-11-27_en), published by the Joint Research Centre on 27 November 2025, integrates AI competence into all its areas.

In Spain, the curriculum already asks for it without naming AI. [Royal Decree 217/2022](https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2022-4975) (in Spanish), setting the minimum teaching requirements for compulsory secondary education (ESO), lays down as a descriptor of digital competence searching “taking into account criteria of validity, quality, currency and reliability” and selecting results “critically”; in linguistic communication, cross-checking information from different sources “evaluating its reliability and relevance”. The [INTEF guide on the use of AI in education](https://intef.es/Noticias/nueva-version-de-la-guia-sobre-el-uso-de-la-inteligencia-artificial-en-el-ambito-educativo/) (in Spanish), in its version 2.0 of September 2026, highlights students’ AI literacy among its novelties. Among the regional guides the paper has reviewed, the most explicit is the Catalan one: the *[Orientacions per a l’ús de la intel·ligència artificial als centres educatius](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/21753/53605)* (in Catalan), [explained in the paper’s Library](pieza:2026-11-02/cat-orientacions-ia), ask teachers to verify what AI generates and to design activities that require interpretation and a personal stance.

For Spanish and Catalan there is a recent finding. Antoni Badia, Lorena Becerril and Marta López-Costa, of the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya, studied with Escola Pia de Catalunya the use of generative AI by 3,700 ESO and sixth-form students at 17 Catalan state-subsidised private schools. According to the [UOC note of 18 June 2026](https://www.uoc.edu/es/news/2026/solo-diez-por-ciento-alumnos-escolares-verifican-iag) (in Spanish), only 10% say they always verify the information in the answers, 23.8% often, 32.9% sometimes, 21.7% rarely and 11.5% never. The authors conclude that verification “is the big weak point”, and the third of their ten recommendations is to teach verification explicitly, with cross-checking sources as part of the task. In ChatGPT-IA-edu, that decalogue was judged [very apt for schools](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/50367).

The difficulty did not begin with chatbots. The Stanford History Education Group, which became the independent organisation [Digital Inquiry Group](https://inquirygroup.org/history) in 2024, assessed 3,446 US high-school students between June 2018 and May 2019 in the report “[Students' Civic Online Reasoning](https://inquirygroup.org/students-civic-online-reasoning)”: 52% took a blurry video as “strong evidence” of electoral fraud, and only three students traced its origin, which was in Russia.

The good news is that, in one study, it was learned quickly. Joel Breakstone, Sam Wineburg and four other researchers published in February 2021, in the [Harvard Kennedy School Misinformation Review](https://misinforeview.hks.harvard.edu/article/lateral-reading-college-students-learn-to-critically-evaluate-internet-sources-in-an-online-course/), an intervention of four one-hour modules in an online university course. Before it, 3 of the 87 students practised lateral reading (leaving the page and searching for what others say about it); afterwards, 67 did. The authors themselves warn that it is not known how long the change lasts or whether students apply it outside the course. **The results suggest that checking is a habit that can be taught with a method.**

In the groups it has been pointed out that the problem is not only students’ own: [what students are asked to do, verify facts and review errors, is not always done by teachers](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/40911). The answer given in that exchange also works for the classroom: review, keep training and, on a subject you do not master, [ask a more experienced colleague to take a look](https://t.me/ChatGPTedu/40917).

With that, a single session is enough to start, in any subject. The teacher operates the chatbot on the classroom screen, as the UNESCO guide proposes for most of its activities and as the Catalan guidelines require for under-14s, so students do not need an account. The chatbot is asked a question from the syllabus whose answer the group can check, ideally one with dates, figures or names. The class underlines the claims that can be verified, picks two or three and checks them against the textbook, an official source or a search of their own, applying the five questions.

At the end, each claim gets a reasoned verdict: accept, revise or reject, as the European framework proposes, and the class discusses what was at stake in each case. One variation is to ask the chatbot for its sources and check whether they exist and say what is attributed to them. **The aim is not to show that AI fails, but for students to leave with a habit: treating the answer as a lead and getting to the source before using it.**

claves: A chatbot produces plausible text, not checked text: fluency is not accuracy, and its makers warn that it can present false information as fact.
UNESCO’s guide “AI answers. You decide” proposes five questions and the gradation trust, verify or question, with the rule of treating the answer as a lead and not a source.

Evaluating whether an AI answer is accepted, revised or rejected is a competence in the OECD and European Commission framework, linked to PISA 2029, and the LOMLOE curriculum already asks for assessing the reliability of sources.

According to a UOC study of 3,700 Catalan secondary students, only 10% always verify what AI tells them; a study with university students suggests that the lateral-reading habit can be learned in a few sessions.
One session is enough, with the chatbot on the teacher’s screen and no student accounts: underline claims, check them and decide whether to accept, revise or reject them.
